It is the growing connection and dependence of
countries around the world through trade, technology,
and the sharing of ideas. It allows people, money, and
goods to move faster and more easily across national
borders than ever before.

Views globalization as a real, transformative new era
defined by a borderless economy, the decline of the
nation-state, and global cultural convergence.

 Borderless Economy: Believes a single, unified global market
now replaces distinct national economies.

 Declining State Power: Argues that national governments are
losing their authority and relevance as multinational corporations
and global financial forces take over.

 Cultural Homogenization: Predicts the creation of a uniform
global culture driven by Western media, consumer brands, and
technology.

Views the current global integration is deeply
exaggerated, geographically concentrated, and
controlled by powerful nation-states rather than a
borderless economy.

 Overstated Phenomenon: Contends that true globalization is a
myth and that current levels of world trade are not historically
unique compared to the 19th century.

 Centered on Regions: Sees the world economy split into major
regional blocs (such as North America, Europe, and East Asia)
rather than a fully integrated globe.

 Strong National Governments: Maintains that nation-states
remain the primary and most powerful actors in controlling trade
and protecting domestic policies.

Views globalization as a massive, long-term historical
process that fundamentally reorganizes modern
states, societies, and global power. They argue that
while the world is deeply interconnected, the future
path of globalization is open, uncertain, and uneven.

 Profound Social Change: Views globalization as a real, highly
powerful force that deeply alters modern social, political, and
economic life..

 Redefined State Power: Argues that nation-states are not dying
out, but are instead changing their roles and finding new ways to
exercise authority.

 Uncertain and Uneven Future: Rejects a fixed path, seeing
globalization as an open-ended process that creates complex
patterns of global winners and losers.
Early Roots and the First Wave

Ancient & Archaic Networks: The Silk Road and Spice Routes, connecting
Asian, African, and European markets.

Age of Discovery: 15th-to-18th-century European maritime exploration
launched the Columbian Exchange and transatlantic trade.

19th-Century Wave (1870–1914): Driven by the Industrial Revolution,
steamships, railroads, and the telegraph created the first peak of deep
international economic integration. This wave collapsed due to World War I
and the Great Depression.
The Post-WWII Revival and Contemporary Era

Bretton Woods & Global Institutions (1940s): The International Monetary Fund
(IMF) and the World Bank are twin global institutions created at the 1944
Bretton Woods conference in Washington, D.C.

The Shipping Container (1956): Standardized freight shipping dramatically cut
transport costs and accelerated physical commerce.

Digital & Late 20th-Century Integration: The fall of the Soviet Union, free-
market trade policies, and the birth of the internet paved the way for hyper-
connected modern digital economies.
